ACL Repair & Reconstruction
ACL Repair & Reconstruction is a specialized orthopedic procedure for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries , common in athletes and active individuals. The ACL is crucial for knee stability, pivoting, and movement , and injuries can lead to instability, pain, and difficulty performing sports or daily activities . Under the guidance of Dr. Nithin Kumar Bejjanki , this procedure restores knee stability and function using advanced surgical techniques and personalized rehabilitation programs .
Symptoms & Conditions Treated
Treatment Options
Procedure Details
FAQs & Recovery
ACL Repair & Reconstruction is recommended for patients experiencing:
Knee instability or giving way during movement
Pain, swelling, or stiffness after injury
Limited mobility affecting daily activities or sports
ACL tears due to trauma, sports injuries, or accidents
Associated injuries like meniscus or cartilage damage
The procedure is designed to restore knee function, prevent further injury, and enable safe return to sport .
Treatment may include:
ACL repair for partial tears or suitable cases
ACL reconstruction using grafts (autograft or allograft) for complete tears
Simultaneous repair of meniscus or cartilage if required
Minimally invasive arthroscopic techniques for precise reconstruction
Post-surgical rehabilitation programs to restore strength, flexibility, and stability
The choice of treatment depends on injury severity, patient age, activity level, and long-term goals .
Preoperative Assessment: Clinical evaluation, MRI imaging, and patient counseling
Anesthesia: General or regional anesthesia based on patient needs
Surgical Procedure: Arthroscopic reconstruction using grafts to replace or repair the torn ACL
Closure & Dressing: Small incisions closed with sutures, knee bandaged
Postoperative Rehabilitation: Structured physiotherapy focusing on range of motion, strength, and gradual return to activity
Patients typically experience improved knee stability, reduced pain, and faster recovery with modern surgical techniques.
Q1: How long does recovery take? A: Full recovery typically takes 6–9 months , depending on patient adherence to rehabilitation.
Q2: Can I return to sports? A: Yes, with structured rehab and gradual progression , athletes can return safely to pre-injury activities.
Q3: Is ACL surgery painful? A: Mild discomfort is managed with medications and physiotherapy ; most patients tolerate the procedure well.
Q4: What are the advantages of reconstruction? A: Restores knee stability, prevents further injury, and allows safe return to sports.
Q5: Will knee function fully return? A: With proper rehabilitation, most patients regain full mobility, strength, and stability .
ACL Repair & Reconstruction is a safe, effective, and athlete-focused procedure that restores knee stability, mobility, and confidence.

Ankle Injury Treatments
Ankle Injury Treatments focus on diagnosing, managing, and rehabilitating injuries of the ankle joint , including sprains, fractures, ligament tears, and tendon injuries . The ankle is a weight-bearing joint essential for walking, running, and sports , making prompt and effective treatment crucial to prevent long-term instability or arthritis. Under the care of Dr. Nithin Kumar Bejjanki , patients benefit from advanced diagnostics, minimally invasive procedures, and personalized rehabilitation programs , ensuring pain relief, restored mobility, and safe return to daily activities or sports .
Symptoms & Conditions Treated
Treatment Options
Procedure Details
FAQs & Recovery
Ankle Injury Treatments address patients experiencing:
Pain, swelling, or bruising after trauma
Instability or recurrent ankle sprains
Ligament or tendon tears
Fractures of the ankle bones
Achilles tendon injuries
Post-traumatic arthritis or chronic ankle pain
Difficulty walking or performing sports activities
The aim is to restore strength, stability, and full functional mobility in the ankle joint.
Non-Surgical / Conservative Approaches:
Immobilization using splints, casts, or braces
Pain management with medications or anti-inflammatory therapy
Physiotherapy for strength, balance, and flexibility
Activity modification to reduce stress and prevent further injury
Surgical / Advanced Interventions:
Ligament reconstruction for chronic instability
Tendon repair (e.g., Achilles or peroneal tendons)
Arthroscopic surgery for cartilage or bone injuries
Fracture fixation using plates, screws, or rods
Regenerative therapies like PRP or stem cell injections
Treatment is tailored to injury type, severity, patient age, and activity level .
Comprehensive Assessment: Clinical evaluation, imaging (X-ray, MRI, or CT)
Treatment Planning: Selecting conservative or surgical approach based on diagnosis
Surgical Intervention (if needed): Repair or reconstruction of ligaments, tendons, or bones
Postoperative Care: Immobilization, pain management, and early physiotherapy
Rehabilitation: Gradual weight-bearing, strengthening, and balance exercises
Follow-Up: Monitoring healing, functional recovery, and prevention of recurrence
Patients benefit from expert care, precise intervention, and structured rehabilitation to regain full ankle function efficiently.
Q1: How long does recovery take for ankle injuries? A: Recovery varies: 4–6 weeks for minor sprains, 3–6 months for surgical repair.
Q2: Can I return to sports after ankle surgery? A: Gradual return is possible with physiotherapy and functional strengthening , usually 3–6 months post-op .
Q3: How is ankle stability restored? A: Through ligament repair, tendon reconstruction, and structured rehabilitation to rebuild strength and balance.
Q4: Are non-surgical treatments effective? A: Yes, mild sprains or minor injuries often heal with immobilization, therapy, and activity modification .
Q5: How can future injuries be prevented? A: Maintain strength, flexibility, and proprioception exercises , wear supportive footwear, and avoid high-risk activities initially.

Arthroscopy for Ankle & Elbow
Arthroscopy for Ankle & Elbow is a minimally invasive orthopedic procedure used to diagnose and treat joint injuries and disorders in the ankle and elbow. Using a small camera (arthroscope) and specialized instruments through tiny incisions, surgeons can repair ligaments, tendons, cartilage, and remove damaged tissue without extensive open surgery. Under the expertise of Dr. Nithin Kumar Bejjanki , patients benefit from precise interventions, faster recovery, and personalized rehabilitation , ensuring pain relief, improved mobility, and early return to activity or sports .
Symptoms & Conditions Treated
Treatment Options
Procedure Details
FAQs & Recovery
Arthroscopy for Ankle & Elbow addresses patients with:
Persistent joint pain or swelling
Limited range of motion
Ligament or tendon injuries (e.g., lateral ankle ligaments, elbow ulnar collateral ligament)
Cartilage or bone damage
Joint instability or recurrent sprains
Inflammation, loose bodies, or impingement
Post-traumatic or degenerative joint conditions
The treatment aims to restore function, relieve pain, and prevent further joint degeneration .
Non-Surgical / Conservative Approaches:
Physiotherapy to improve strength, flexibility, and range of motion
Pain management using medications or injections
Activity modification to reduce joint stress
Surgical / Arthroscopic Interventions:
Debridement of damaged tissue or loose fragments
Ligament or tendon repair
Removal of inflamed bursae or scar tissue
Capsular release for stiffness
Cartilage repair or microfracture procedures
Regenerative therapies such as PRP injections to enhance healing
Treatment is personalized based on joint, injury severity, and patient activity level .
Preoperative Assessment: Clinical evaluation and imaging (X-ray, MRI, or CT)
Anesthesia: Local, regional, or general anesthesia depending on procedure
Surgical Procedure: Small incisions are made; arthroscope and instruments are used for precise repair
Closure & Dressing: Tiny incisions closed with sutures or adhesive strips; joint bandaged
Postoperative Rehabilitation: Early mobilization, physiotherapy for strength, flexibility, and function
Follow-Up: Regular monitoring to ensure proper healing, joint stability, and pain-free motion
Arthroscopy allows less tissue damage, minimal scarring, and faster return to work or sports compared to traditional open surgery.
Q1: How long is recovery after arthroscopy? A: Most patients regain functional movement within 4–6 weeks , full strength in 2–3 months .
Q2: Is arthroscopy painful? A: Mild discomfort is expected and managed with pain medications and structured physiotherapy .
Q3: Can I return to sports? A: Gradual return is possible within 2–3 months , depending on joint and procedure performed.
Q4: Are there risks? A: Rare risks include infection, stiffness, or nerve irritation , minimized with skilled surgical technique.
Q5: How effective is arthroscopy compared to open surgery? A: Equally effective with faster recovery, minimal scarring, and lower complication rates .

Introduction
Arthroscopic Bankart Repair is a minimally invasive shoulder repair. Doctors use it to fix shoulder instability, often after a dislocation. This surgery helps restore strength and prevent future injuries. Many people choose this option because it uses small cuts and special tools. As a result, recovery is often quicker than with open surgery. In this guide, you will learn about the procedure, recovery, and tips for a healthy shoulder.
What is Arthroscopic Bankart Repair?
Arthroscopic Bankart Repair is a type of shoulder dislocation surgery. It treats a Bankart lesion, which is a tear in the shoulder’s labrum. The labrum is a ring of cartilage that helps keep the shoulder joint stable. When it tears, the shoulder may slip out of place. This surgery uses a tiny camera and small tools to repair the tear. Because it is minimally invasive, there is less pain and a faster recovery.
Symptoms and Causes of Shoulder Instability
Shoulder instability means your shoulder can slip or dislocate easily. This often happens after an injury or repeated strain. Common symptoms include:
Pain or aching in the shoulder
A feeling that the shoulder is loose or may pop out
Weakness when lifting or moving the arm
Clicking or catching sensations
Most often, a Bankart lesion occurs after a shoulder dislocation. Sports injuries, falls, or accidents can cause this problem. Sometimes, repeated overhead movements, like throwing, can also lead to instability.
How is the Diagnosis Made?
Doctors use several steps to diagnose shoulder instability and decide if Arthroscopic Bankart Repair is needed. First, they ask about your symptoms and medical history. Next, they perform a physical exam to check for pain, weakness, or looseness. Often, imaging tests help confirm the diagnosis. These may include:
X-rays to check for bone damage
MRI scans to see soft tissues like the labrum
CT scans in some cases for detailed images
According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, these steps help doctors plan the best treatment.
Step-by-Step Overview of the Arthroscopic Bankart Repair Procedure
Arthroscopic Bankart Repair is a common minimally invasive shoulder repair. Here is what usually happens during the surgery:
You receive anesthesia to keep you comfortable.
The surgeon makes small cuts around your shoulder.
A tiny camera (arthroscope) goes into the joint for a clear view.
Special tools are used to clean the area and find the tear.
The surgeon attaches the torn labrum back to the bone using small anchors and stitches.
The tools and camera are removed, and the cuts are closed with stitches or tape.
This procedure usually takes one to two hours. Because it is less invasive, most people go home the same day.
Recovery Timeline and What to Expect After Surgery
Recovery after Arthroscopic Bankart Repair takes time, but most people return to normal activities. Here is a general timeline:
First week: Your arm will be in a sling. Pain and swelling are common, but medicine helps.
Weeks 2–6: You will start gentle movements with your therapist’s help. The sling stays on most of the time.
Weeks 6–12: You can begin more active exercises. Strength and motion improve slowly.
After 3 months: Most daily activities are safe. Sports or heavy lifting may take longer.
Always follow your doctor’s advice. Recovery times can vary based on your age, health, and the extent of the injury.
Tips for Rehabilitation and Lifestyle Adjustments
Rehabilitation is key to a strong recovery after Bankart lesion treatment. Here are some helpful tips:
Attend all physical therapy sessions as scheduled.
Do your home exercises every day, as your therapist instructs.
Wear your sling as directed to protect your shoulder.
Avoid lifting heavy objects or sudden arm movements.
Eat healthy foods to support healing.
Get enough sleep and rest.
With patience and care, you can regain strength and motion. If you notice new pain or swelling, contact your doctor right away.
Prevention of Future Shoulder Injuries
After shoulder dislocation surgery, it is important to protect your joint. Here are some ways to prevent future injuries:
Warm up before sports or exercise.
Strengthen your shoulder muscles with regular exercises.
Use proper techniques when lifting or playing sports.
Avoid activities that strain your shoulder too soon after surgery.
Listen to your body and rest when needed.
According to the CDC, staying active and strong helps lower the risk of repeat injuries.
Conclusion
Arthroscopic Bankart Repair is a safe and effective treatment for shoulder instability, allowing most patients to return to their favourite activities with proper care. However, every case is unique, and tailored guidance is essential for the best outcomes.

What is Rheumatoid Arthritis?
Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-lasting disease that causes swelling and pain in the joints. Unlike common joint pain, this condition happens when the body’s immune system attacks healthy joint tissue. Because of this, joints can become stiff, swollen, and painful. Early signs of rheumatoid arthritis often start slowly, so it is important to know what to look for. Recognizing rheumatoid arthritis symptoms early can help you get the right treatment and prevent joint damage.
Common Symptoms of Rheumatoid Arthritis
Many people wonder about the main signs of this disease. While symptoms can vary, some are seen more often. For example, joint pain and swelling are common. In addition, you may notice other changes in your body. Here are the most frequent rheumatoid arthritis symptoms:
Joint pain, especially in the hands, wrists, or knees
Swelling and warmth around the joints
Stiffness, often worse in the morning or after resting
Fatigue or feeling very tired
Low-grade fever
Loss of appetite
Sometimes, these symptoms can come and go. However, if they last for weeks, it may be a sign of rheumatoid arthritis.
Early Warning Signs to Watch For
It is important to spot early signs of rheumatoid arthritis. Early treatment can slow the disease and protect your joints. So, what should you look for? Here are some early warning signs:
Stiffness in small joints, like fingers or toes, lasting over an hour in the morning
Redness or warmth in the joints
Feeling tired even after enough rest
Unexplained weight loss
Minor swelling that does not go away
Even if these signs seem mild, they should not be ignored. Early action can make a big difference.
How Rheumatoid Arthritis Symptoms Progress
At first, symptoms may be mild and affect only a few joints. Over time, though, the disease can spread to more joints. For instance, pain may start in the fingers and later move to the wrists, knees, or ankles. As the disease gets worse, joints may lose their shape or function. In some cases, people may notice lumps under the skin near the joints. Because symptoms can change, it is important to keep track of any new problems.
When to See a Doctor
Sometimes, joint pain is caused by other problems. However, if you notice any of the symptoms listed above, it is wise to see a doctor. You should seek help if:
Joint pain or swelling lasts more than a few weeks
Stiffness is worse in the morning and lasts over an hour
You feel tired or unwell for no clear reason
Everyday tasks become hard due to joint pain
Doctors can run tests to find the cause and suggest the best treatment. According to the CDC, early diagnosis can help prevent long-term joint damage.
Tips for Managing Symptoms at Home
While medical care is important, some home steps can help manage symptoms. For example, you can:
Rest your joints when they feel sore
Use cold packs to reduce swelling

What is Tendonitis?
Tendonitis is a common condition that affects many people. It happens when a tendon, which connects muscle to bone, becomes inflamed or irritated. Because tendons help your body move, tendonitis can cause pain and limit movement. Often, this condition affects the shoulders, elbows, wrists, knees, or heels. Early care can help prevent long-term problems. According to the CDC, tendonitis is often caused by overuse or injury.
Common Causes of Tendonitis
Many things can lead to tendonitis. However, some causes are more common than others. Understanding these can help you avoid the condition. For example, repetitive movements or sudden injuries often trigger tendonitis. In addition, certain sports or jobs increase your risk. Age can also play a role, as tendons lose flexibility over time.
Repetitive motions, such as typing or playing sports
Sudden injuries or falls
Poor posture or body mechanics
Not warming up before exercise
Age-related tendon wear and tear
Certain medical conditions, like diabetes or arthritis
Symptoms of Tendonitis
Recognizing tendonitis symptoms early can help you seek treatment quickly. Most people notice pain near a joint. However, other signs may also appear. If you have any of these symptoms, it is important to rest and seek advice.
Pain or tenderness near a joint
Swelling or warmth in the area
Stiffness, especially in the morning
Difficulty moving the affected joint
Mild redness or a feeling of heat
Sometimes, symptoms get worse with activity. On the other hand, rest may help reduce pain.
How is Tendonitis Diagnosed?
Doctors use several steps to diagnose tendonitis. First, they ask about your symptoms and medical history. Next, they examine the affected area. Sometimes, they may order tests to rule out other problems. For example, an X-ray or ultrasound can help check for injuries. In most cases, a physical exam is enough. However, extra tests can confirm the diagnosis if needed.
Treatment Options for Tendonitis
There are many tendonitis treatment options available. Early treatment can speed up recovery and prevent further injury. Most people start with simple steps at home. However, some may need medical care. According to the CDC and Mayo Clinic, common treatments include:
Resting the affected area
Applying ice to reduce swelling
Taking over-the-counter pain relievers
Using a brace or support
Physical therapy exercises
In rare cases, steroid injections or surgery
For ongoing pain, orthopedic care for tendonitis may be needed. Your doctor can help you choose the best treatment plan.
Prevention and Lifestyle Tips
While tendonitis can be painful, you can take steps to prevent it. Making small changes in your daily routine can help protect your tendons. For example, always warm up before exercise. In addition, use proper techniques during sports or work.
Stretch before and after activity
Take breaks from repetitive tasks
Use the right equipment and shoes
Maintain good posture
Strengthen muscles around joints
Listen to your body and rest when needed
By following these tips, you can lower your risk and learn how to prevent tendonitis.
When to See an Orthopedic Specialist
Sometimes, tendonitis does not improve with home care. If pain lasts more than a few days, it is time to see a doctor. In addition, severe swelling, redness, or loss of movement are warning signs. Orthopedic care for tendonitis can help you recover faster and avoid complications. Your specialist may suggest advanced treatments or therapy.
Conclusion
Tendonitis is a common condition, but early care can make a significant difference. By understanding the causes, symptoms, and treatment options, you can take control of your health. Treatment Options

Osteoarthritis or cartilage degeneration
Ligament or tendon injuries
Chronic joint pain and inflammation
Sports injuries with slow healing
Post-traumatic joint damage
Early-stage arthritis or joint stiffness
Desire to avoid invasive surgery while restoring function
The goal is to stimulate natural tissue repair, reduce pain, and improve mobility .

Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Injections: Concentrated growth factors to accelerate tissue healing

Bone Marrow Aspirate Concentrate (BMAC): Enhances repair in joint, tendon, and ligament injuries
Exosome Therapy: Promotes cellular regeneration and reduces inflammation

Follow-Up: Monitoring pain relief, functional improvement, and tissue regeneration progress
These therapies often accelerate healing and improve joint function , reducing the need for invasive surgical procedures.

Q5: How long do the effects last? A: Results vary; most patients experience long-term pain relief and functional improvement , especially when combined with rehab.

Tibial Osteotomy (Knee Realignment) is a specialized orthopedic procedure designed to correct knee alignment issues , relieve joint pain , and delay or prevent the progression of osteoarthritis . It involves surgically cutting and reshaping the tibia (shinbone) to redistribute weight across the knee joint, reducing stress on damaged cartilage. Under the expertise of Dr. Nithin Kumar Bejjanki , patients benefit from precise surgical planning, minimally invasive techniques, and personalized rehabilitation programs , enabling pain relief, improved mobility, and enhanced joint function .

Treatment Options
Procedure Details

Medial or lateral knee pain due to misalignment
Early osteoarthritis affecting one side of the knee
Bow-legged (varus) or knock-kneed (valgus) deformities
Instability or uneven weight distribution in the knee
Limited mobility and difficulty performing daily activities
Persistent pain despite conservative treatments
The goal is to realign the knee, relieve stress on damaged cartilage, and preserve joint longevity .
Non-Surgical / Conservative Approaches:
Pain management with medications or injections
Physical therapy to strengthen muscles supporting the knee
Bracing and activity modification to reduce joint stress
Weight management to relieve pressure on the knee
Surgical / Advanced Interventions:
High Tibial Osteotomy (HTO): Corrects varus deformity
Distal Tibial Osteotomy (DTO): Corrects valgus deformity
Arthroscopic-assisted realignment: Minimally invasive techniques for precise correction
Combination with cartilage or ligament repair to optimize knee function
The procedure is personalized based on the severity of deformity, cartilage condition, patient age, and activity level .
Preoperative Assessment: Clinical evaluation, X-rays, and CT scans to determine precise alignment
Surgical Planning: Selection of osteotomy type and corrective angle
Surgical Procedure: Bone is cut, realigned, and fixed with plates or screws
Closure & Dressing: Incision closed, knee immobilized with a brace or bandage
Postoperative Rehabilitation: Gradual weight-bearing, physiotherapy to restore strength, flexibility, and gait
Follow-Up: Regular imaging and monitoring to ensure proper healing and alignment
Tibial osteotomy reduces pressure on affected knee compartments, improves function, and delays the need for total knee replacement .

Q2: Will I regain normal knee function? A: Most patients experience significant pain relief and improved mobility , especially with structured rehab.
Q3: Is the surgery painful? A: Mild to moderate discomfort is expected and managed with medications and physiotherapy .
Q4: Can I return to sports? A: Low-impact activities can resume after 3–6 months ; high-impact sports may require caution.
Q5: Are there risks associated with the procedure? A: Rare risks include infection, delayed bone healing, or hardware irritation , minimized with expert surgical technique.
